correctness.rationale: Reconstruction from the published exact prime-power Fibonacci ranks produces an exact exponent map preserving the 5-exponent. Its invariant quadrant gives the coordinatewise hitting maximum and all four boundary regimes are separately checked. A uniform O(L^2) count for 3D weighted lattice simplices, bounded-width exponent strips, and exact inclusion-exclusion yield the claimed uniform O(1/log X) CDF error; survival integration yields the mean. Standalone independently computed modular ranks agree for all 192 prescribed triples, with further 10,000 exponent-pair cross-checks; finite checks are not used as infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The full lawful 2023 source establishes one-dimensional powers-of-two hitting times and rank iterate properties but not a smooth-height-sampled hitting-time distribution; an exact nonlinear two-exponent reduction plus a weighted-simplex limit are needed. The 2014 and 2020 primary texts address respectively self-divisibility counts and absence of higher cycles, not the new uniform CDF. No identical/dominating statement surfaced in the actual semantic and primary searches. Remaining journal-version/unindexed priority risks are explicit, so this is evidence-based not absolute uniqueness.
residual_risks: The full 2025 publisher text of the same paper was inaccessible, although its lawfully accessible 2023 preprint was materially read; a new result in a later version is possible.
Earlier unindexed statistical treatments of Fibonacci ranks could contain the same calculation.
The novelty is a derived exact statistical limit, not a new formula for prime-power rank itself.

value.rationale: The five-smooth domain is the natural invariant terminal core in the 2014/2023 convergence proofs. The theorem resolves a motivated distributional question for actual first fixed-point times, with sharp support, a uniform convergence rate, nondegenerate explicit CDF, and mean coefficient. The two-exponent exact dynamics link the original arithmetic map to a simplex-counting law; the result is not merely finite tabulation or the already-known existence of fixed points.
